By the late 1960s, the wreckage of termination was unmistakable: terminated communities lost hospitals, tax-exempt land bases, and sustainable timber economies almost overnight. Yet out of reservation leadership and urban Native communities shaped by Relocation emerged a vibrant Indigenous civil-rights movement insisting that Tribes must govern themselves.

In 1970, President Richard Nixon formally repudiated termination, inaugurating the modern era of **tribal self-determination**: federal policy recognizing that Tribal nations—not distant federal bureaucrats—should design, direct, and deliver governance and public services for their own peoples. Congress anchored this shift in the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act of 1975 (often called 'Public Law 93-638'), enabling Tribes to contract or compact directly with federal agencies to operate their own police, schools, clinics, and social services using federal dollars. Congress also enacted restoration laws reviving federal recognition for many terminated nations, including the Menominee and Klamath.

questions.prompt: How did the 1975 Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act transform day-to-day governance in Indian Country?
choices: It shifted control of all reservation schools and clinics permanently from Washington to state governors.
It required Tribal councils to obtain annual approval from neighboring mayors before adopting local budgets.
It restarted the Dawes Act allotment process so individual citizens could sell trust land without restrictions.
It enabled Tribes to contract directly with federal agencies to run their own police, health, and school programs.
questions.explanation: The 1975 Act operationalized tribal self-determination by allowing Tribes to contract and compact directly to run federally funded services rather than leaving administration to federal bureaucrats.

questions.prompt: What happened to many Tribal nations like the Menominee and Klamath after the federal government repudiated termination in 1970?
choices: They remained permanently barred from ever re-establishing a formal relationship with the federal government.
Congress passed restoration statutes reviving their federal recognition and rebuilding their government-to-government status.
The Supreme Court merged all terminated western communities into a single federally run metropolitan territory.
State supreme courts granted them foreign diplomatic immunity under international treaty arbitration panels.
questions.explanation: Following the repudiation of termination policy, Congress enacted restoration statutes reinstating federal recognition for dozens of terminated Tribes, including the Menominee and Klamath.

chunks.title: Living With Overlapping Eras on Today's Legal Map
chunks.content_markdown:
Looking back across the twentieth century reveals a golden rule of Federal Indian Law: new policy eras rarely erase old statutes overnight. Congress repudiated termination policy decades ago and committed to tribal self-determination, restoring dozens of terminated nations and supporting Tribes running their own institutions. Yet Public Law 280 remains active law in its designated states—creating a split national map where state authorities handle most reservation prosecutions in Public Law 280 states, whereas federal and Tribal authorities carry primary responsibility elsewhere.

Keeping that split map in mind prepares us to step directly inside modern courthouses. With inherent sovereignty, the Marshall Trilogy, treaties, plenary power, and two centuries of policy swings now under our belt, we are ready to unpack how jurisdiction actually works day to day—starting with Tribal courts and the intricate rules deciding who prosecutes crime in Indian Country.

questions.prompt: Why does Federal Indian Law operate on a 'split map' for criminal enforcement across different states today?
choices: Because the Supreme Court struck down all federal criminal statutes west of the Rocky Mountains in 1975.
Because only Tribal nations located east of the Mississippi River maintain their own local police departments.
Because Public Law 280 still assigns primary criminal jurisdiction to designated states while other states follow federal-tribal rules.
Because the 1975 Self-Determination Act required half of all states to surrender criminal authority to county boards.
questions.explanation: Even though modern policy favors tribal self-determination, Public Law 280 was never broadly repealed, leaving designated states with state criminal jurisdiction while other states follow federal-tribal baselines.

questions.prompt: Which sequence accurately captures the mid-to-late twentieth-century shift in federal Indian policy?
choices: Termination, Relocation, and Public Law 280 in the 1950s gave way to Tribal Self-Determination and restorations starting in the 1970s.
Tribal Self-Determination in the 1950s gave way to mandatory Termination and Relocation nationwide during the 1980s.
Public Law 280 restored every terminated Tribe in 1953 before Bryan v. Itasca County abolished Tribal courts in 1976.
President Nixon launched the Termination era in 1970 before Congress halted federal recognition entirely in 1975.
questions.explanation: Federal policy swung from the 1950s Termination, Relocation, and Public Law 280 era to President Nixon's 1970 repudiation and the modern Tribal Self-Determination era.

sections.title: 7. Tribal Courts & the Indian Country Criminal Jurisdictional Maze
sections.summary: Maps how more than 300 modern Tribal justice systems operate alongside federal and state prosecutors, and why criminal authority in Indian Country turns on location plus the Indian or non-Indian status of both offender and victim. Synthesizes the Major Crimes Act, the General Crimes Act, statutory civil-rights protections in Tribal courts, Oliphant v. Suquamish Indian Tribe's implicit-divestiture limit on prosecuting non-Indians, and modern congressional restorations including the Violence Against Women Act's special tribal criminal jurisdiction over non-Indians for covered offenses.

chunks.title: One Parking Lot, Three Possible Prosecutors
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine an assault occurring outside a small grocery store inside an Indian reservation in a non–Public Law 280 state. In an ordinary town, dialing 911 leads predictably to local police and the county prosecutor. In Indian Country, however, nobody knows which courthouse holds authority until three threshold questions are answered: Did the offense happen inside Indian Country? Is the accused person an Indian or a non-Indian? And is the victim an Indian or a non-Indian?

Today, more than 300 Tribal justice systems operate nationwide—ranging from formal trial and appeals courts staffed by law-trained judges to restorative peacemaking courts rooted in Indigenous legal traditions. Under the 1968 Indian Civil Rights Act (ICRA), Congress applied most core fair-trial guarantees—such as due process, free speech, and bans on unreasonable searches—as federal statutory limits inside Tribal courts. Yet Tribal courts share the criminal landscape with federal and state systems along sharply divided lines.

questions.prompt: Which three threshold factors typically determine who has criminal jurisdiction over an offense in a non–Public Law 280 state?
choices: The value of stolen property, the suspect's voter registration, and the date of state admission.
Whether the site is Indian Country, the defendant's Indian or non-Indian status, and the victim's status.
Whether the local mayor approves, the age of the courthouse, and the highway distance to Washington.
The defendant's state tax bracket, the victim's employer, and whether a federal bank sits nearby.
questions.explanation: Criminal jurisdiction in Indian Country hinges on a three-part threshold inquiry: location inside Indian Country, whether the offender is Indian or non-Indian, and whether the victim is Indian or non-Indian.

questions.prompt: How do modern Tribal justice systems operate alongside the 1968 Indian Civil Rights Act (ICRA)?
choices: Tribal courts are restricted strictly to traffic tickets and cannot hear criminal or family cases.
ICRA abolished all traditional Indigenous peacemaking forums and merged them into county trial courts.
Tribal courts operate solely as federal magistrate branches appointed directly by the President.
Over 300 Tribal systems blend formal trials and traditional methods while enforcing statutory ICRA rights.
questions.explanation: More than 300 diverse Tribal court systems handle criminal and civil matters using both modern procedures and customary peacemaking while applying ICRA's statutory rights protections.

chunks.title: Federal Reach: The General Crimes Act and Major Crimes Act
chunks.content_markdown:
To see how federal prosecutors entered reservation criminal law, start with two nineteenth-century statutes. First, the General Crimes Act (18 U.S.C. 1152) extends general federal criminal law into Indian Country primarily for interracial offenses—crimes committed by an Indian against a non-Indian, or by a non-Indian against an Indian—while explicitly carving out crimes committed by one Indian against another, which originally remained solely inside Tribal justice systems.

That carve-out sparked a landmark turn in 1883. When a Lakota man named Crow Dog killed a rival leader on the Great Sioux Reservation, the Tribal community resolved the dispute through traditional restitution—yet federal officials arrested and sentenced him to hang. In *Ex parte Crow Dog*, the Supreme Court freed him because Congress had never granted federal criminal power over Indian-on-Indian offenses. Congress quickly responded with the **Major Crimes Act** of 1885 (18 U.S.C. 1153), granting federal courts concurrent (shared) jurisdiction alongside Tribal courts over specifically listed serious felonies—including murder, kidnapping, arson, and felony assault—committed by Indians in Indian Country.

questions.prompt: What criminal authority did Congress create when it passed the Major Crimes Act of 1885?
choices: Federal court jurisdiction over specified serious felonies committed by Indians inside Indian Country.
Exclusive state court authority to prosecute every misdemeanor occurring anywhere on Tribal trust land.
A constitutional ban preventing Tribal courts from hearing any case involving two citizens of the same Tribe.
Authority for county sheriffs to enforce local municipal ordinances inside federally recognized reservations.
questions.explanation: Enacted after Ex parte Crow Dog, the Major Crimes Act gave federal courts concurrent jurisdiction to prosecute enumerated major felonies committed by Indians in Indian Country.

questions.prompt: How does the General Crimes Act differ from the Major Crimes Act in Indian Country?
choices: The General Crimes Act applies strictly to environmental violations committed by non-Indian corporations.
The General Crimes Act applies exclusively inside the six mandatory Public Law 280 states.
The General Crimes Act primarily covers interracial offenses and exempts Indian-on-Indian crimes, unlike the Major Crimes Act.
The General Crimes Act strips federal prosecutors of power whenever a victim is a non-Indian visitor.
questions.explanation: The General Crimes Act extends federal criminal law mainly to interracial crimes in Indian Country (carving out Indian-on-Indian offenses), whereas the Major Crimes Act reaches listed felonies by Indians even against Indian victims.

chunks.title: Oliphant, Implicit Divestiture, and Walking the Criminal Matrix
chunks.content_markdown:
Now ask the crucial question: can a Tribal court prosecute a *non-Indian* who commits a crime on the reservation? In *Oliphant v. Suquamish Indian Tribe* (1978), two non-Indian residents arrested on the Port Madison Reservation challenged Tribal criminal jurisdiction. Even though neither Congress nor any treaty had stripped Tribes of that power, the Supreme Court held that Tribes lacked inherent criminal authority over non-Indians. The Court relied on **implicit divestiture**: the doctrine that Tribes silently lost certain external powers over nonmembers as an implied consequence of becoming 'domestic dependent nations.'

Walk through the classic non–Public Law 280 criminal matrix that resulted. For Indian-on-Indian crimes, Tribal courts handle all offenses while federal courts share power over Major Crimes. For Indian-on-non-Indian crimes, both Tribal and federal courts hold authority. For non-Indian-on-Indian crimes, federal prosecutors held authority while *Oliphant* blocked Tribal prosecution. And for non-Indian-on-non-Indian crimes, state courts—not Tribal or federal courts—prosecute.

questions.prompt: What reasoning did the Supreme Court use in Oliphant v. Suquamish Indian Tribe to bar Tribal criminal prosecutions of non-Indians?
choices: It cited an explicit 1789 treaty clause in which every Tribe surrendered authority over visitors.
It ruled that the 1968 Indian Civil Rights Act permanently closed all Tribal criminal dockets.
It concluded that reservations ceased to qualify as Indian Country whenever highways crossed them.
It applied implicit divestiture, holding that dependent status silently stripped criminal power over non-Indians.
questions.explanation: Without pointing to an explicit congressional statute or treaty surrender, Oliphant invoked implicit divestiture to hold that Tribes lost inherent criminal jurisdiction over non-Indians.

questions.prompt: Under the classic non–Public Law 280 criminal matrix after Oliphant, which sovereign prosecutes a crime committed by a non-Indian against another non-Indian on a reservation?
choices: The Tribal court prosecutes under its inherent criminal authority and the reserved-rights doctrine.
The state court prosecutes, as neither federal nor Tribal criminal statutes cover that crime.
The federal court prosecutes exclusively under its felony authority in the Major Crimes Act.
No court may prosecute until Congress passes a special federal bill authorizing a trial.
questions.explanation: Under Supreme Court precedent (United States v. McBratney), state courts—not Tribal or federal courts—hold criminal jurisdiction over crimes committed by non-Indians solely against non-Indians on reservations.

chunks.title: Closing the Gap: Duro Fix, TLOA, and VAWA Restorations
chunks.content_markdown:
*Oliphant* left a dangerous public-safety gap: when non-Indian offenders assaulted Native victims on reservations, Tribal police could only detain suspects briefly while waiting for distant federal prosecutors who often lacked capacity to prosecute lower-level or complex cases. Congress responded with three targeted restorations.

First, after a 1990 ruling briefly barred Tribes from prosecuting citizens of *other* Tribes, Congress enacted the 'Duro fix,' affirming inherent Tribal criminal power over *all* Indians—upheld in *United States v. Lara* (2004). Second, the Tribal Law and Order Act of 2010 raised Tribal sentencing ceilings up to three years per offense when enhanced defense safeguards apply. Most notably, the Violence Against Women Act (VAWA) reauthorizations of 2013 and 2022 recognized **special tribal criminal jurisdiction**: restored Tribal authority to prosecute non-Indians in Indian Country for covered offenses—including domestic violence, sexual violence, child violence, and assaults on Tribal justice personnel—paired with licensed judges, appointed defense counsel, and inclusive juries.

questions.prompt: What authority does VAWA's 'special tribal criminal jurisdiction' restore to qualifying Tribal courts?
choices: Unlimited power for Tribal courts to try non-Indians for any offense occurring anywhere inside the state.
Power for state prosecutors to sit as voting judges on Tribal appellate panels during felony trials.
Power for Tribal courts to prosecute non-Indians in Indian Country for covered offenses with enhanced due-process safeguards.
Power for Tribal councils to waive federal criminal oversight under the Major Crimes Act by simple majority vote.
questions.explanation: VAWA's 2013 and 2022 reauthorizations recognized special tribal criminal jurisdiction allowing Tribes that meet enhanced due-process requirements to prosecute non-Indians for covered reservation offenses.

questions.prompt: What did Congress affirm through the 'Duro fix,' later upheld by the Supreme Court in United States v. Lara?
choices: Tribes retain inherent criminal jurisdiction over all Indians in Indian Country, including citizens of other Tribes.
Federal prosecutors must obtain written consent from a state governor before invoking the General Crimes Act.
Non-Indian defendants prosecuted under VAWA may elect to transfer their cases automatically to county court.
Tribal courts may impose unlimited prison terms without providing defense counsel or law-trained judges.
questions.explanation: The Duro fix recognized Tribes' inherent criminal authority over nonmember Indians in Indian Country, and United States v. Lara upheld Congress's power to lift judicial restrictions on that inherent authority.

chunks.title: From Criminal Limits to Everyday Civil Power
chunks.content_markdown:
Look back at the intricate criminal map we just assembled. Deciding who prosecutes an offense inside Indian Country never reduces to a single blanket rule—it weaves together location, offender and victim status, Public Law 280 variations, the General Crimes Act, the Major Crimes Act, *Oliphant*'s implicit-divestiture barrier, and Congress's modern restorations such as VAWA's special tribal criminal jurisdiction.

Pay special attention to *Oliphant*'s driving idea: **implicit divestiture**, the notion that Tribal nations lost certain authority over *nonmembers* even without an explicit act of Congress. That concept did not remain confined to criminal law for long. Just three years after *Oliphant*, the Supreme Court carried implicit-divestiture thinking straight into everyday civil disputes—confronting how Tribal nations regulate businesses, enforce zoning, hear civil lawsuits, and protect their own treasuries on checkerboard reservations where nonmembers live, drive, and sign contracts.

questions.prompt: Why does the Major Crimes Act not completely displace Tribal courts when an Indian commits a serious felony against another Indian on a reservation?
choices: Because the Major Crimes Act applies exclusively to non-Indian visitors passing along federal highways.
Because federal Major Crimes authority operates concurrently with the Tribe's own inherent criminal jurisdiction.
Because the Supreme Court struck down the Major Crimes Act when it decided Ex parte Crow Dog.
Because Tribal courts automatically take exclusive control whenever a federal prosecutor declines a case.
questions.explanation: Under the separate-sovereigns framework, Tribal courts retain inherent criminal authority concurrently alongside federal jurisdiction under the Major Crimes Act.

questions.prompt: Which concept from Oliphant v. Suquamish Indian Tribe soon expanded beyond criminal prosecutions into civil and regulatory disputes?
choices: The 1871 congressional ban on ratifying formal land-cession treaties with southeastern Tribes.
The 1975 contracting framework allowing Tribes to run their own health clinics and local schools.
The requirement that non-Indian property owners pay personal property taxes to Minnesota counties.
Implicit divestiture—limiting Tribal authority over nonmembers even where Congress has not explicitly acted.
questions.explanation: Implicit divestiture—first used in Oliphant to limit Tribal criminal power over non-Indians—became the conceptual springboard for Supreme Court limits on Tribal civil authority over nonmembers.

sections.title: 8. Civil Jurisdiction, Tribal Court Exhaustion & Sovereign Immunity
sections.summary: Turns from criminal enforcement to everyday civil disputes, contracts, zoning, and regulatory power across checkerboard reservations. Unpacks Montana v. United States—the baseline rule limiting Tribal civil authority over nonmembers on non-Indian fee land along with its two vital exceptions for consensual relationships and conduct threatening Tribal political integrity, economic security, or health and welfare—before exploring the tribal court exhaustion doctrine requiring litigants to let Tribal courts weigh their own jurisdiction first, and tribal sovereign immunity shielding Tribes from unconsented lawsuits unless waived or clearly abrogated by Congress.

chunks.title: Who Sets the Fishing Rules on a Checkerboard River?
chunks.content_markdown:
Picture a sparkling trout river winding right through the Crow Reservation in Montana. Remember the checkerboard land tenure left behind by the Dawes Act: one stretch of riverbank sits on Crow Tribal trust land, while another stretch sits on unrestricted private fee land owned by non-Indian ranchers inside reservation borders. In the 1970s, the Crow Tribe enacted an ordinance barring nonmembers from hunting and fishing anywhere within reservation limits.

On Tribal trust land, a Tribe's power to exclude visitors or regulate their conduct is broad and well settled. The harder question was what happened when nonmembers stood on *non-Indian fee land* inside reservation borders. Could the Crow Tribe regulate their hunting and fishing there too? In *Montana v. United States* (1981), that riverside conflict produced the foundational framework that governs Tribal civil regulatory and courtroom authority over nonmembers across Indian Country today.

questions.prompt: Why did the Crow Reservation dispute in Montana v. United States hinge on land ownership status?
choices: Because the Crow Tribe claimed ownership of public fishing docks located in neighboring states.
Because Congress had repealed all federal conservation statutes across western rivers in 1975.
Because nonmembers were hunting and fishing on interior non-Indian fee land rather than Tribal trust land.
Because Montana was one of the original six mandatory states designated under Public Law 280.
questions.explanation: While Tribes retain broad authority to regulate nonmembers on Tribal trust land, Montana confronted whether that civil regulatory power extends to nonmembers on non-Indian fee land inside a reservation.

questions.prompt: How does Tribal civil regulatory authority generally compare on Tribal trust land versus non-Indian fee land?
choices: Tribal authority is broad on Tribal trust land, whereas authority over nonmembers on non-Indian fee land faces stricter limits.
Tribal authority applies strictly to non-Indian fee land, whereas state counties regulate all Tribal trust parcels.
Tribal authority is identical across both types of land whenever a state highway passes through the reservation.
Tribal councils possess no civil regulatory authority anywhere unless Congress passes a new annual license.
questions.explanation: Tribes hold strong inherent regulatory power over activities on Tribal trust land, whereas civil jurisdiction over nonmembers on non-Indian fee land is restricted by the Montana framework.

chunks.title: Montana v. United States and Its Two Vital Exceptions
chunks.content_markdown:
Carrying *Oliphant*'s implicit-divestiture reasoning into civil law, the Supreme Court in *Montana v. United States* announced a general baseline rule: Tribal nations ordinarily lack civil regulatory power—and, as the Court later confirmed in *Strate v. A-1 Contractors*, civil courtroom jurisdiction—over nonmembers on non-Indian fee land inside a reservation.

Crucially, however, the Court carved out two **Montana exceptions** where Tribal civil authority remains intact even on non-Indian fee land. Under the first exception, a Tribe may regulate nonmembers who enter **consensual relationships** with the Tribe or its citizens, such as commercial dealings, contracts, leases, or business licenses. Under the second exception, a Tribe retains authority when nonmember conduct on fee land **threatens or directly affects** the Tribe's political integrity, economic security, or health and welfare. Think of the two exceptions in everyday terms as 'voluntary business deal' and 'serious community threat.'

questions.prompt: What are the two 'Montana exceptions' under which a Tribe may exercise civil authority over nonmembers on non-Indian fee land?
choices: Historic European land grants and state governor delegations issued prior to 1871.
Consensual relationships with the Tribe or citizens, and conduct directly threatening Tribal integrity, security, or welfare.
Minor highway traffic infractions and federal postal deliveries crossing exterior reservation boundaries.
Public Law 280 opt-in agreements and state municipal zoning ordinances ratified by county voters.
questions.explanation: Under Montana v. United States, Tribes retain civil authority over nonmembers on interior fee land when either a consensual relationship exists or the conduct threatens Tribal political integrity, economic security, or health and welfare.

questions.prompt: How did Strate v. A-1 Contractors expand the reach of the Montana v. United States framework?
choices: It abolished both Montana exceptions whenever a nonmember owned commercial agricultural machinery.
It applied Montana exclusively to federal criminal prosecutions brought under the Major Crimes Act.
It granted Tribal courts automatic civil jurisdiction over every highway collision nationwide.
It held that Montana's baseline limits and two exceptions govern Tribal civil courtroom jurisdiction as well as regulation.
questions.explanation: Strate confirmed that a Tribe's civil adjudicatory (courtroom) authority over nonmembers on non-Indian fee land generally tracks its civil regulatory authority under Montana.

chunks.title: Testing the Montana Exceptions on Everyday Scenarios
chunks.content_markdown:
Walk through three concrete scenarios on non-Indian fee land inside a reservation to see how courts apply the *Montana* exceptions. First, imagine a non-Indian construction firm signing a commercial contract with a Tribe to renovate a community center, then walking off the job mid-project. Because the contractor voluntarily entered a commercial contract with the Tribe, the first Montana exception—consensual relationship—supports Tribal civil jurisdiction over disputes tied to that deal.

Second, imagine a non-Indian salvage yard operating on an interior fee parcel that leaks hazardous chemicals toward the groundwater aquifer supplying the reservation's drinking water. Because that contamination directly endangers Tribal health and welfare, the second exception supports Tribal regulatory protection. Third, imagine two non-Indian motorists colliding on a state highway running across a reservation (as in *Strate*): neither driver entered a consensual commercial deal with the Tribe, and an ordinary traffic accident does not catastrophically threaten Tribal self-government, so neither exception applies.

questions.prompt: A non-Indian vendor leases booth space from a Tribal agency on interior fee land and breaches the lease. Which rule best supports Tribal civil jurisdiction over the contract claim?
choices: Montana's first exception, because the vendor voluntarily entered a consensual commercial relationship with the Tribe.
Montana's baseline bar, which prohibits Tribal courts from ever hearing commercial disputes involving nonmembers.
The Major Crimes Act, which assigns all commercial lease breaches inside reservations to Tribal juries.
The doctrine of discovery, which transfers every leased business asset automatically to federal marshals.
questions.explanation: Signing a commercial lease with a Tribal agency is a classic consensual relationship triggering Montana's first exception for disputes connected to that relationship.

questions.prompt: Why did two non-Indian drivers colliding on a state highway inside a reservation fall outside Tribal civil court jurisdiction in Strate v. A-1 Contractors?
choices: Because state highways running through reservations automatically erase the surrounding reservation borders.
Because Tribal courts are barred by the Indian Civil Rights Act from ever awarding civil money damages.
Because the crash involved neither a consensual Tribal relationship nor a serious threat to Tribal governance.
Because federal law requires all motor-vehicle injury lawsuits nationwide to be filed in federal district court.
questions.explanation: On a state highway treated like non-Indian fee land, a routine crash between nonmembers triggered neither a consensual relationship nor a direct threat to Tribal political integrity or welfare.

chunks.title: Who Decides First? Tribal Court Exhaustion and Sovereign Immunity
chunks.content_markdown:
Two vital doctrines shield Tribal courts and Tribal governments in civil litigation. First is **tribal court exhaustion** (*National Farmers Union*, *Iowa Mutual*): suppose a nonmember sued in Tribal court believes the Tribal court lacks jurisdiction under *Montana*. May that litigant skip the Tribal judge and run straight to federal district court for an injunction—a court order halting the case? Normally, no. Out of 'comity'—mutual institutional respect between separate court systems—federal courts require challengers to let the Tribal trial and appellate courts examine their own jurisdiction first, unless Tribal jurisdiction is plainly absent or pursued in bad faith.

Second is **tribal sovereign immunity** (*Kiowa Tribe*, *Michigan v. Bay Mills Indian Community*): as sovereign governments, Tribal nations cannot be sued in federal, state, or Tribal court—even over off-reservation commercial ventures—unless the Tribe clearly waives its immunity or Congress unmistakably abrogates it. That shield protects Tribal public treasuries and self-governance from crippling lawsuits.

questions.prompt: What does the 'tribal court exhaustion' doctrine generally require when a nonmember disputes a Tribal court's civil jurisdiction?
choices: The nonmember must first submit the jurisdictional objection to the state governor for binding arbitration.
The Tribal court must automatically dismiss any civil lawsuit the moment a nonmember objects in writing.
The federal district court must stay all state courts statewide until Congress revises 18 U.S.C. 1151.
The litigant must let Tribal trial and appellate courts rule on jurisdiction first before seeking federal court review.
questions.explanation: Grounded in federal-tribal comity, tribal court exhaustion requires litigants to give the Tribal court system the first opportunity to evaluate its own jurisdiction (absent narrow exceptions).

questions.prompt: Under Kiowa Tribe and Bay Mills, how does 'tribal sovereign immunity' protect a federally recognized Tribe in civil litigation?
choices: It shields Tribal governments solely from injury lawsuits inside reservations while permitting all contract suits freely.
It bars unconsented suits against Tribes—on or off reservation—absent clear Tribal waiver or congressional abrogation.
It immunizes individual non-Indian tourists from state traffic tickets whenever they drive through Tribal land.
It permits state legislatures to revoke a Tribe's legal immunity whenever a commercial venture turns a profit.
questions.explanation: Tribal sovereign immunity bars lawsuits against Tribal governments—both on and off the reservation—unless the Tribe clearly waives immunity or Congress unmistakably abrogates it.

chunks.title: Civil Sovereignty in Action—and Approaching Modern Flashpoints
chunks.content_markdown:
Look at how Section 8's civil toolkit operates in the real world. On Tribal trust land, Tribal regulatory and judicial power is robust; on non-Indian fee land inside reservations, *Montana*'s general limit yields to the two Montana exceptions—consensual relationships and direct threats to Tribal governance, economy, or health and welfare. Meanwhile, tribal court exhaustion gives Tribal judges first review of jurisdictional challenges, and tribal sovereign immunity guards Tribal treasuries—which is why outside lenders and contractors routinely negotiate carefully written, limited waivers of immunity (or seek court orders halting unlawful actions by officials) rather than walking away from Tribal business deals.

Notice, though, a quiet assumption sitting beneath both our criminal map and our civil map: everyone assumes we already know *where* a reservation's outer boundary actually lies. In 2020 and 2022, two blockbuster Supreme Court cases out of Oklahoma shattered that assumption and sparked the fiercest jurisdictional flashpoints of our era.

questions.prompt: How do outside businesses and lenders typically handle tribal sovereign immunity when negotiating major commercial contracts with a Tribe?
choices: They ask neighboring state legislatures to pass local ordinances overriding the Tribe's sovereign status.
They file preemptive federal lawsuits asking judges to abolish sovereign immunity for all commercial contracts.
They negotiate explicit, carefully scoped contractual waivers of immunity and agreed dispute procedures upfront.
They ignore immunity entirely because sovereign immunity disappears whenever a contract exceeds one year.
questions.explanation: Because Tribes may voluntarily waive immunity, commercial partners routinely negotiate clear, limited contractual waivers specifying remedies and forums in advance.

questions.prompt: Why does knowing the exact exterior boundary of a reservation matter so deeply across both criminal and civil Federal Indian Law?
choices: Because reservation boundaries define Indian Country, triggering federal, Tribal, and Montana jurisdictional rules.
Because Tribal sovereign immunity disappears completely the moment a Tribe signs a contract off the reservation.
Because state legislatures automatically redraw reservation boundaries every ten years following the federal census.
Because tribal court exhaustion applies strictly to disputes arising in downtown state capitals outside reservations.
questions.explanation: Reservation boundaries define the geographic scope of Indian Country, which determines whether federal criminal statutes, Tribal authority, and civil frameworks like Montana apply.

sections.title: 9. Contemporary Jurisdictional Flashpoints: McGirt & Castro-Huerta
sections.summary: Examines two landmark 2020s Supreme Court rulings from Oklahoma that illustrate the live doctrinal tension between treaty textualism and state-sovereignty pragmatism. Walks through McGirt v. Oklahoma—holding that allotment, statehood, and non-Indian settlement never erase a reservation unless Congress unmistakably enacts reservation disestablishment—and contrasts it with Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta, which narrowed Worcester's territorial barrier by recognizing concurrent state criminal jurisdiction alongside federal authority over non-Indians committing crimes against Indian victims in Indian Country.

chunks.title: Can Nearly Half of Oklahoma Still Be an Indian Reservation?
chunks.content_markdown:
Imagine a defendant convicted in Oklahoma state court for a grave crime committed in Tulsa making an astonishing claim: Oklahoma had no legal authority to prosecute him at all, because he is a citizen of a federally recognized Tribe and eastern Oklahoma is still the Muscogee (Creek) Nation's 1866 treaty reservation.

For more than a century after Oklahoma became a state in 1907, state officials assumed the historic reservations of the Creek and neighboring Tribes had long since vanished through allotment, waves of non-Indian settlement, and statehood. Yet when lawyers searched federal statutes from the past hundred years, they faced an extraordinary fact: Congress had never passed a single law explicitly erasing the Creek Reservation's exterior boundary. That clash between century-old treaty text and everyday state assumptions reached the Supreme Court in *McGirt v. Oklahoma* (2020), igniting the biggest jurisdictional flashpoint in modern Federal Indian Law.

questions.prompt: What core legal argument did the defendant raise in McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020) to challenge his state court conviction?
choices: That Congress had designated Oklahoma a mandatory Public Law 280 state barring federal prosecutions.
That Congress never erased the 1866 Creek Reservation, leaving eastern Oklahoma outside state Major Crimes power.
That the Major Crimes Act expired automatically once Oklahoma gained formal statehood status in 1907.
That Tulsa municipal criminal ordinances superseded both nineteenth-century federal treaties and Oklahoma state statutes.
questions.explanation: Because the defendant was a Tribal citizen prosecuted for a Major Crimes Act offense inside the 1866 Creek borders, he argued Oklahoma lacked jurisdiction since Congress never disestablished the reservation.

questions.prompt: Why had Oklahoma state officials long assumed the historic Creek Reservation no longer existed before McGirt?
choices: Because the Muscogee (Creek) Nation had signed a 1954 termination agreement surrendering federal recognition.
Because the Supreme Court had struck down all southeastern removal treaties during the 1930s.
Because federal courts had declared Tulsa a non-Indian federal enclave completely exempt from treaties.
Because allotment, extensive non-Indian settlement, and decades of statehood practices led officials to treat it as gone.
questions.explanation: Over a century of allotment, non-Indian population growth, and state criminal prosecutions led Oklahoma officials to assume the reservation had disappeared even without a congressional disestablishment statute.

chunks.title: Reservation Disestablishment: Only Congress Can Erase a Treaty Border
chunks.content_markdown:
To decide *McGirt*, the Supreme Court applied a strict constitutional rule governing **reservation disestablishment**—the legal termination or reduction of a reservation's official exterior boundaries. Under settled precedent (*Solem v. Bartlett*), allotment, changing local demographics, or decades of state enforcement cannot dissolve a reservation by themselves. Because Congress established reservations through treaties and statutes, **only Congress** possesses authority to disestablish a reservation—and only by expressing clear statutory intent to wipe away its borders.

Picture a national park whose borders Congress drew by statute: even if private cabins are built inside and county crews pave the roads, the park's legal boundary remains intact until Congress explicitly votes to redraw it. Opening with the ringing line 'On the far end of the Trail of Tears was a promise,' Justice Neil Gorsuch's 5–4 majority ruled that because Congress never clearly disestablished the Creek Reservation, it remained Indian Country under federal law.

questions.prompt: Under McGirt v. Oklahoma, who holds legal authority to enact 'reservation disestablishment' and erase a reservation's borders?
choices: Only Congress, and only through clear statutory expression rather than implied historical assumptions.
Any state legislature whose non-Indian population outnumbers Tribal citizens inside reservation lines.
Federal trial judges whenever local demographics shift significantly following an allotment statute.
State governors acting jointly with county prosecutors after fifty years of uninterrupted state policing.
questions.explanation: McGirt reaffirmed that only Congress can disestablish a reservation, and courts may not infer disestablishment from allotment, demographics, or state practices without clear congressional text.

questions.prompt: Why did Justice Gorsuch's majority opinion reject Oklahoma's reliance on historical non-Indian settlement and past state prosecutions?
choices: Because the Court concluded that Tulsa was actually located inside Kansas rather than Oklahoma.
Because Congress had passed a 2019 statute barring states from citing historical records in court.
Because breaking a treaty promise without congressional authorization—no matter how long practiced—cannot erase statutory borders.
Because allotment automatically converts every privately owned non-Indian parcel back into federal trust land.
questions.explanation: Applying strict textualism, the majority held that unlawful or mistaken assumptions by state officials over many decades cannot substitute for an actual act of Congress disestablishing a reservation.

chunks.title: McGirt's Ripple Effects—and Intergovernmental Cooperation
chunks.content_markdown:
Watch what happened on the ground once *McGirt v. Oklahoma* took effect. Because the Muscogee (Creek) Reservation—and soon, through follow-up Oklahoma appellate rulings applying *McGirt*'s reasoning, the historic reservations of the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Seminole, and Quapaw Nations—remained legally intact, roughly forty percent of Oklahoma was recognized as Indian Country for federal criminal-law purposes.

Immediately, Oklahoma state courts lost jurisdiction over crimes committed by Indians within those borders, shifting thousands of prosecutions into federal U.S. Attorney offices and rapidly expanding Tribal court systems. Crucially, however, many alarmist headlines missed what *McGirt* did *not* do: private non-Indian homeowners did not lose their deeds or see their land seized, because reservation boundaries and private fee ownership are separate legal concepts. Instead, Tribal nations, federal agencies, and many local Oklahoma sheriffs expanded cross-deputization agreements—allowing officers to enforce multiple sovereigns' laws—and dramatically scaled up Tribal prosecutors, police, and courthouses.

questions.prompt: What happened to private non-Indian homeowners' property deeds in eastern Oklahoma after McGirt v. Oklahoma?
choices: Every private home inside the Creek Reservation reverted automatically to federal trust ownership.
Non-Indian homeowners were required to repurchase their land from the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
Private homeowners immediately lost the right to vote in Oklahoma state legislative elections.
Private land deeds stayed intact, because reservation boundary status does not confiscate private fee titles.
questions.explanation: Recognizing exterior reservation boundaries under 18 U.S.C. 1151 governs jurisdiction in Indian Country—it does not take away or alter private individuals' underlying fee titles.

questions.prompt: How did federal, Tribal, and local law-enforcement institutions adapt practically to the post-McGirt caseload shift?
choices: All criminal prosecutions in eastern Oklahoma were permanently suspended pending a constitutional amendment.
Tribes expanded courts and police capacity while using cross-deputization pacts with federal and local partners.
Congress immediately enacted Public Law 280 across Oklahoma without seeking consent from any Tribe.
Tribal courts transferred all Indian-on-Indian felony trials exclusively to neighboring Texas state judges.
questions.explanation: Following McGirt, Tribal nations rapidly expanded their justice systems and worked with federal and local agencies through cross-deputization and cooperative policing agreements.

chunks.title: Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta: Narrowing Worcester's Territorial Wall
chunks.content_markdown:
Just two years after *McGirt*, a reshaped Supreme Court delivered a dramatic counter-swing in *Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta* (2022). Victor Manuel Castro-Huerta, a non-Indian man, was convicted in Oklahoma state court of severely neglecting his Cherokee stepdaughter in Tulsa—inside Indian Country after *McGirt*. Under the classic *Worcester v. Georgia* understanding, lawyers had long assumed that outside Public Law 280 states, federal prosecutors—not states—held exclusive jurisdiction over crimes committed by non-Indians against Indian victims in Indian Country.

In a sharp 5–4 decision written by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, the Court narrowed *Worcester*'s territorial barrier. Declaring that 'Indian country is part of the State, not separate from the State,' the majority recognized **concurrent state criminal jurisdiction** alongside federal authority to prosecute non-Indians who commit crimes against Indian victims in Indian Country—unless preempted—meaning overridden or blocked—by federal statute or unlawfully infringing Tribal self-government. In a blistering dissent, Justice Gorsuch accused the majority of abandoning nearly two centuries of *Worcester* precedent.

questions.prompt: What new jurisdictional rule did the 5–4 Supreme Court announce in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta (2022)?
choices: States hold exclusive authority to prosecute every crime committed by Tribal citizens on trust land.
States are permanently barred from prosecuting any non-Indian defendants anywhere inside federal reservation borders.
States share concurrent criminal jurisdiction with federal prosecutors over non-Indians committing crimes against Indians in Indian Country.
Tribal courts automatically gain unlimited criminal jurisdiction over every non-Indian resident living across Oklahoma.
questions.explanation: Castro-Huerta held that states share concurrent criminal jurisdiction with the federal government to prosecute non-Indians who commit crimes against Indian victims in Indian Country (absent preemption or unlawful infringement).

questions.prompt: Why did Justice Gorsuch's dissent argue that Castro-Huerta marked a sharp break with Worcester v. Georgia?
choices: Because Worcester had long treated Indian Country as insulated from general state law absent congressional delegation.
Because Worcester had granted Oklahoma exclusive authority over all criminal trials inside Indian Territory.
Because Castro-Huerta formally overturned the Major Crimes Act and closed federal district courts in Tulsa.
Because Worcester had required states to share concurrent criminal authority with Congress on every reservation.
questions.explanation: Whereas Worcester established a territorial presumption keeping state law out of Indian Country unless Congress authorized it, Castro-Huerta inverted that presumption for non-Indian-on-Indian crime.

chunks.title: Two Visions of Sovereignty Colliding on the Modern Court
chunks.content_markdown:
Set *McGirt* and *Castro-Huerta* side by side and you can see a live constitutional tug-of-war inside today's Supreme Court. *McGirt* champions treaty and statutory textualism—strict adherence to written legal text—refusing to invent reservation disestablishment out of later state convenience. *Castro-Huerta* champions state-sovereignty pragmatism: treating Indian Country as part of the surrounding state and recognizing concurrent state criminal jurisdiction over non-Indian-on-Indian crimes unless federal law blocks it.

Keep two essential boundaries crystal clear: even after *Castro-Huerta*, states still lack general authority to prosecute *Indian* defendants for crimes committed inside Indian Country (outside Public Law 280), and *McGirt*'s reservation borders remain legally intact. With the Court so sharply divided over federalism and Tribal sovereignty, legal observers held their breath the very next year when a sweeping constitutional attack reached the justices targeting a cornerstone federal statute protecting Native families—bringing all ten pieces of our Federal Indian Law toolkit to a dramatic finale.

questions.prompt: Which critical jurisdictional limit remained intact even after the Supreme Court's decision in Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta?
choices: States gained automatic authority to disestablish any reservation whenever state prosecutors request it.
Non–Public Law 280 states still generally lack criminal jurisdiction over Indian defendants committing crimes in Indian Country.
Federal prosecutors lost all authority under the General Crimes Act to prosecute non-Indian offenders.
Tribal courts were stripped of their inherent authority to try Indian-on-Indian offenses inside reservations.
questions.explanation: Castro-Huerta addressed only non-Indian defendants committing crimes against Indian victims; outside Public Law 280, states still do not hold general criminal jurisdiction over Indian defendants in Indian Country.

questions.prompt: How do McGirt v. Oklahoma and Oklahoma v. Castro-Huerta illustrate a live doctrinal tension on the modern Supreme Court?
choices: Both rulings unanimously transferred all reservation governance to the Department of the Interior.
Both rulings held that nineteenth-century treaties automatically expire after one hundred years.
McGirt eliminated federal plenary power while Castro-Huerta restored pre-1871 treaty-making authority.
McGirt enforced strict treaty textualism protecting reservation borders, while Castro-Huerta expanded state criminal reach inside them.
questions.explanation: Together, the two 5–4 decisions highlight competing judicial philosophies—strict textual adherence to congressional treaty boundaries in McGirt versus broader state territorial authority in Castro-Huerta.

sections.title: 10. ICWA, Haaland v. Brackeen & Modern Nation-to-Nation Governance
sections.summary: Brings the entire Federal Indian Law toolkit together in modern family law, governance, and intergovernmental partnership. Explores the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) and the Supreme Court's 7–2 decision in Haaland v. Brackeen upholding Congress's Article I authority and rejecting Tenth Amendment anti-commandeering challenges, then surveys how Tribal nations exercise sovereignty today through modern constitutions, taxation, natural resource co-management, diversified economic development including the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA), and formal nation-to-nation relations.

chunks.title: A Crisis in Family Courts and the Indian Child Welfare Act
chunks.content_markdown:
In the mid-1970s, congressional investigations uncovered a devastating national crisis: state child-welfare agencies and private adoption networks were removing between one-quarter and one-third of all Native American children from their homes, placing roughly eighty-five percent of them with non-Native families even when loving Tribal relatives stood ready to raise them. Tribal leaders warned that stripping away an entire generation threatened the very survival of Tribal nations.

Congress responded by passing the **Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA)** of 1978. ICWA sets minimum federal standards for state foster-care and adoption cases involving children who are citizens of—or eligible for citizenship in—a federally recognized Tribe. It affirms exclusive Tribal court jurisdiction for children living on reservations, creates a strong presumption for transferring off-reservation cases to Tribal courts, requires 'active efforts' to reunite families before terminating parental rights, and establishes placement preferences prioritizing extended family, the child's Tribe, and other Native families unless good cause favors another placement.

questions.prompt: What historic crisis prompted Congress to enact the Indian Child Welfare Act (ICWA) in 1978?
choices: A dispute over which states could collect federal highway fuel taxes near western reservations.
A shortage of federal district judges available to try Major Crimes Act felony cases.
Widespread removal of Native children from their families into non-Native homes by state and private systems.
A wave of state statutes attempting to close down Tribal bingo halls across California and Florida.
questions.explanation: Congress passed ICWA after hearings revealed that state agencies and private adoption networks were removing 25% to 35% of Native children from their families, largely into non-Native placements.

questions.prompt: Which core safeguard does the Indian Child Welfare Act establish for covered child-custody proceedings?
choices: Minimum federal standards including Tribal court jurisdiction protections, active family-reunification efforts, and placement preferences.
An absolute ban prohibiting any state family court from ever issuing emergency protective orders for children.
A requirement that every child living in a western state be enrolled automatically in a neighboring Tribe.
A federal mandate transferring all municipal public schools nationwide to Bureau of Indian Affairs control.
questions.explanation: ICWA protects Native children and Tribal continuity through Tribal court jurisdiction rules, heightened 'active efforts' standards to keep families together, and family- and Tribe-centered placement preferences.

chunks.title: Haaland v. Brackeen: Constitutional Stress-Test of Indian Law
chunks.content_markdown:
Decades later, Texas and non-Native prospective adoptive families launched a sweeping constitutional attack on ICWA that threatened the foundations of Federal Indian Law. They raised three claims: Congress lacked Article I power over state family-court proceedings; ICWA violated the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering rule—barring Congress from forcing state officials to enforce federal programs; and ICWA's placement preferences were unconstitutional racial discrimination.

In *Haaland v. Brackeen* (2023), a 7–2 Supreme Court decisively upheld ICWA. Writing for the majority, Justice Amy Coney Barrett reaffirmed Congress's broad Article I plenary authority over Indian affairs. The Court rejected the anti-commandeering claims because ICWA's rules apply neutrally to state agencies and private parties alike, and state courts must apply supreme federal law. Finally, the Court dismissed the equal-protection claim for lack of legal standing—the constitutional rule requiring a plaintiff to show a real injury caused by the defendant that the court can actually fix—because federal officials do not enforce state placement orders, leaving *Morton v. Mancari* undisturbed.

questions.prompt: How did the 7–2 Supreme Court rule on Congress's authority and Tenth Amendment anti-commandeering claims in Haaland v. Brackeen?
choices: It struck down ICWA in full, ruling that family law belongs exclusively to state legislatures without exception.
It upheld ICWA, reaffirming Congress's broad Article I Indian-affairs power and rejecting anti-commandeering objections.
It limited ICWA solely to federal military bases while invalidating its placement rules in state courts.
It overturned Morton v. Mancari and ordered Congress to apply strict racial scrutiny to all Indian statutes.
questions.explanation: In Haaland v. Brackeen, the Court decisively reaffirmed Congress's plenary Article I power over Indian affairs and held that ICWA did not violate the Tenth Amendment's anti-commandeering doctrine.

questions.prompt: How did the Supreme Court handle the equal-protection challenge to ICWA's placement preferences in Haaland v. Brackeen?
choices: It declared ICWA's placement preferences unconstitutional under strict racial scrutiny nationwide.
It ruled that state governors may individually decide whether equal-protection rules apply to ICWA.
It formally abolished the Indian canons of treaty construction for all post-1978 federal statutes.
It dismissed the claim on standing grounds without reaching the merits, leaving Morton v. Mancari intact.
questions.explanation: Because federal defendants do not enforce state-court placement preferences, the Court held the challengers lacked Article III standing on equal protection, leaving Mancari undisturbed.

chunks.title: Modern Tribal Governance: Constitutions, Taxation & Fiscal Reality
chunks.content_markdown:
Stepping beyond headline Supreme Court battles, how do the 570+ Tribal nations actually govern every day? Across Indian Country, Tribes operate dynamic constitutional governments—many revising older 1934 IRA templates or drafting modern constitutions with independent judiciaries, environmental agencies, elections commissions, and citizen bills of rights.

Like federal and state governments, Tribes also exercise inherent sovereign power to levy taxes on economic activity within their borders—collecting sales, hotel, or resource-extraction taxes to fund schools, roads, clinics, and emergency responders. Yet Tribal finance faces a persistent structural obstacle called 'dual taxation.' Unlike state counties, Tribes cannot broadly tax non-Indian fee parcels, and when a state *also* taxes non-Indian businesses operating inside a reservation, outside investors can face double taxation that drives away jobs. Rather than fighting endless lawsuits, many Tribes and states today negotiate cooperative tax-sharing compacts that split revenues fairly and encourage reservation business growth.

questions.prompt: What practical governance problem does 'dual taxation' create for many modern Tribal economies?
choices: Overlapping Tribal and state taxes on non-Indian reservation commerce can discourage outside business investment.
Federal law requires Tribal citizens to pay identical personal income taxes to two different neighboring states.
Constitutional limits prohibit Tribes from collecting any form of sales or hotel tax on Tribal trust land.
State courts routinely confiscate Tribal tax treasuries to reimburse federal Bureau of Indian Affairs loans.
questions.explanation: When both a Tribe and a state impose taxes on non-Indian businesses operating inside a reservation, the resulting dual-taxation burden can deter investment—prompting many Tribes and states to sign tax-sharing compacts.

questions.prompt: How are many Tribal nations evolving their constitutional and fiscal institutions in the twenty-first century?
choices: By surrendering their elected councils to become ordinary municipal towns chartered by county governments.
By replacing written Tribal codes entirely with uniform state statutes drafted by neighboring legislatures.
By updating constitutions, strengthening independent Tribal courts, and negotiating tax-sharing compacts with states.
By halting local taxation altogether and relying solely on nineteenth-century federal land-cession payments.
questions.explanation: Modern Tribal nations actively strengthen self-governance through constitutional reform, independent judiciaries, inherent taxation, and intergovernmental tax compacts.

chunks.title: Economic Development, IGRA & Natural Resource Co-Management
chunks.content_markdown:
When people hear 'Tribal economic development,' many think only of casinos—yet modern Tribal economies span renewable energy, forestry, agriculture, tourism, manufacturing, healthcare, and federal contracting. Gaming itself operates within a structured federal framework: the **Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA)** of 1988, enacted after *California v. Cabazon Band* held that states could not ban Tribal gaming where similar state gambling was permitted.

IGRA sorts gaming into three tiers: traditional social games (Class I, solely Tribal), bingo and player-against-player card games like poker (Class II, Tribal-federal), and casino-style gaming (Class III), which requires a negotiated Tribal-state compact. Crucially, IGRA requires net gaming revenues to fund Tribal government operations, general welfare, schools, clinics, and economic diversification—not private shareholder dividends. Beyond commerce, Tribes also lead natural resource co-management—partnering with federal and state agencies to jointly steward salmon runs, watersheds, wildfire resilience, and sacred public landscapes such as Bears Ears National Monument.

questions.prompt: Under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (IGRA), what must a Tribe generally negotiate before operating Class III casino-style gaming, and how must net revenues be used?
choices: A bilateral treaty ratified by the U.S. Senate, with revenues distributed solely to private Wall Street investors.
A county zoning permit approved by local mayors, with revenues transferred into federal highway trust accounts.
A unanimous federal court injunction, with revenues reserved exclusively for out-of-state tourism advertising.
A Tribal-state compact, with net revenues directed toward Tribal government operations, public welfare, and economic development.
questions.explanation: IGRA requires a negotiated Tribal-state compact for Class III casino gaming and mandates that net revenues support Tribal governance, public services, general welfare, and economic development.

questions.prompt: What does modern 'natural resource co-management' involve for federally recognized Tribal nations?
choices: Selling ancestral watersheds to private utilities in exchange for temporary municipal electricity discounts.
Partnering with federal or state agencies to jointly steward shared fisheries, forests, waters, and public lands.
Surrendering treaty-reserved hunting and fishing rights whenever state wildlife budgets run short.
Transferring all reservation timber and mineral decisions exclusively to county planning boards.
questions.explanation: Natural resource co-management brings Tribal nations—often backed by reserved treaty rights and Indigenous ecological knowledge—into formal shared stewardship with federal and state land managers.

chunks.title: Nation-to-Nation Relations and the Living Third Sovereign
chunks.content_markdown:
Zoom out across our entire ten-section arc—from inherent, pre-constitutional sovereignty and the Marshall Trilogy through treaties, plenary power, shifting policy eras, criminal and civil jurisdictional rules, *McGirt*, *Castro-Huerta*, and *Haaland v. Brackeen*. Every doctrine ultimately connects to one unifying framework: **nation-to-nation relations**, the formal government-to-government relationship through which more than 570 Tribal nations engage federal and state counterparts via treaties, formal federal consultation policies, cross-deputization pacts, tax and IGRA compacts, and resource co-management.

Federal Indian Law is neither a dusty historical sidebar nor an isolated specialty—it is a living constitutional laboratory showing how three distinct kinds of sovereigns share one continent under the rule of law. Carrying that three-sovereign lens forward deepens how you read every corner of American public law, from federalism and separation of powers to administrative governance and civil rights.

questions.prompt: What best describes 'nation-to-nation relations' in modern Federal Indian Law?
choices: A ceremonial historical term that ceased to apply once Congress ended formal treaty-making in 1871.
An informal lobbying arrangement between state chambers of commerce and county school boards.
The formal government-to-government partnership linking Tribal nations with federal and state counterparts through consultation and compacts.
An international diplomatic treaty system supervised solely by foreign embassies outside the United States.
questions.explanation: Nation-to-nation relations refers to the ongoing government-to-government partnership through which Tribal nations engage federal and state governments via consultation, compacts, co-management, and sovereign diplomacy.

questions.prompt: Synthesizing the full module, which statement accurately connects Tribal sovereignty to the broader American constitutional system?
choices: Over 570 Tribal nations exercise inherent, pre-constitutional sovereignty as a third sovereign shaped by treaties, plenary power, and evolving jurisdictional rules.
Tribal nations derive all governing authority from state charters enacted during the 1950s termination era and remain wholly subordinate to county laws.
Supreme Court rulings from Worcester through Brackeen have eliminated federal authority over Indian affairs and granted states complete civil and criminal control.
Because Congress halted treaty-making in 1871 and enacted allotment in 1887, Indian Country borders and Tribal courts no longer operate under modern U.S. law.
questions.explanation: Across all ten sections, Federal Indian Law centers on 570+ Tribal nations exercising inherent sovereignty as the third sovereign within a dynamic framework of treaties, congressional plenary power, policy history, and modern intergovernmental governance.
